transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, to be honest with you, it’s because people keep telling me my talking gets all mixed up. I don't always see it that way, but that's what they keep saying to me. Like, I’ll be trying to explain something at work—I clean buildings, you know, sweeping and buffing, so I have this big heavy ring of brass keys—and I try to explain to my supervisor about the keys, because you really have to understand the keys first. But then, to actually get why the keys matter, I have to tell them about the jail, because that's just how the structure of it all works, and then that leads right into the prayer rug, the one with the specific woven pattern that has to face a certain direction, and then of course the chess pieces. Mostly the knights and the bishops, because of the way they move across the board. 

I try to explain how they all go together—the keys, the jail, the prayer rug, the chess pieces—because it’s all connected if you just sit down and listen to the details. I try to lay it all out for them, step by step, giving them all the background they need so it makes sense, but they just look at me like I'm speaking another language. They tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. They say I jump around too much and get tangled up, but I'm just trying to give them the whole picture, you know? But because they can't follow me, and it keeps happening when I try to explain things, they said I had to come down here and see somebody about it.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you noticed your mood being unusually high, euphoric, or irritable, along with having much more energy than usual or needing less sleep?

Well, you know, it’s funny you ask that, because... yeah, I guess "high" is one way to put it, though it feels more like this massive surge of electricity. Like it starts in the soles of my work boots and shoots right up my spine. Lately, there are these times where I just feel so incredibly powerful. I mean, ten feet tall, like I could pick up the heavy-duty floor buffer with one hand and toss it across the room. 

I get to feeling so good, just vibrating with all that energy, that I start laughing out loud—just this big, booming laugh echoing all down the empty hallways. And when I do see people, like the security guards or the night delivery guys, I am talking so loud to them, just booming my voice, telling them everything, because I feel so fantastic and on top of the world. I just want to share how great it all is. 

But... the thing is, and this is where it gets tricky, if one of them interrupts me? Or if my supervisor comes around and questions what I'm doing, or asks why I'm not in a different hallway yet? Man, it is like a switch flips in my chest. I can just snap. I mean, I will shout right in their face over the smallest little thing. Just explode. They ask me to move my cleaning cart two inches to the left and I'm suddenly screaming at them, because they just don't understand the flow I'm in, you know? They question my methods, and I just lose it and yell right at them.
Does this jumping-around, hard-to-follow way of talking happen only during those high-energy, 'electric' periods, or does it also happen at times when your mood feels normal?

Well, see, that's the thing. That's exactly the thing I was trying to explain to my supervisor before he started getting all huffy with me. It’s not just when I'm feeling ten feet tall and full of that electricity. No, sir. Even when I’m just... regular, you know? When I’m just going about my business, pushing the mop bucket, not feeling too high up and not feeling too low down, just kind of coasting through the shift. I can go for weeks like that, just feeling completely normal. But even then, even when my mood is flat as a pancake, I still get the talking thing. Because, well, how can I not? I still have to explain the keys and the chess pieces because... well, because of the things that are still happening. 

Like, even on those calm weeks, and I’m talking a good two, maybe three weeks at a stretch where I'm not shouting or laughing or anything, I still hear him. The man in the vents. He’s always up there, right above the drop ceiling where the ductwork meets the main return line on the third floor. I can hear him whispering about the structure, about how the building is settling, but it's not just settling, it's shifting on purpose. And then there are the people in the offices. Even when I'm calm, I see them doing it. The way they leave their coffee mugs turned exactly 45 degrees toward the door, or the way they tap their security badges against the scanner twice instead of once—they are signaling. They are definitely signaling about me. And when you see all that, when you hear the man in the vents and you see the signals, you have to explain it to people. You have to lay out the whole picture with the jail and the prayer rug so they understand why the mugs are turned that way. So, yeah, it happens even when I'm completely calm, because the signals and the voice, they don't stop just because my mood settles down.

Thinking back over the entire time you've been having these experiences—how long has this all been going on in total, and roughly what proportion of that time have you been in one of those 'electric,' high-energy or irritable periods versus just calm with the voices and signals?

Well, if I really sit back and think about the whole entire timeline of it all... I mean, going all the way back to when the very first things started feeling different, you know, when the keys started feeling heavier in my hand and I first noticed the dust patterns changing in the corners of the hallways... I'd say it's been going on for a long time now. A very long time. Years, really. I can't give you an exact date, because time gets a little slippery when you're working the night shift anyway, but it's been a long haul. 

But as for how much of that time I've been in that... that electric state? That's the real meat of the issue right there, doctor. That's the thing that really wears out the soles of my boots. If I had to break it down, cut the pie into slices, I would say that most of the time—the vast, vast majority of the time since all of this really got going—I have been stuck in those keyed-up stretches. It's like my engine is just revving and revving and nobody knows how to turn the key off. 

During those stretches, which just go on and on, I talk too much. I know I do. I talk to the security guards, I talk to the stray cats in the alley behind the dumpsters, I talk to the mop bucket. And I take on these... these impossible cleaning plans. I mean, I will look at a 40,000 square foot office building and decide that every single baseboard needs to be scrubbed with a toothbrush before the sun comes up, because if they aren't, the whole structural integrity of the building is going to fail. And I feel so driven. Driven like a nail into a piece of hardwood. I just cannot slow down. I push and I push, sweeping and buffing and talking and explaining the chess pieces to anyone who walks by, because the energy just demands it. So, yeah, even though I have those quiet weeks where I just hear the man in the vents and see the mugs turning, those calm periods are really just little islands. The rest of it, the big ocean of it all, is just me being so wound up and electric that I can't even catch my own breath.

I'm sorry, doc, I just realized I've been talking a mile a minute and you're just sitting there looking at me. Did you... did you just ask me another question? I completely missed it if you did. 

It's just exactly like I was saying, when that engine is revving, it gets so incredibly loud in my own head. It's like standing right next to the massive industrial boiler down in the sub-basement when it first kicks on for the winter—just this heavy, roaring, vibrating hum that vibrates right through your ribs and drowns out every single other sound in the room. You could be standing two feet away shouting at me and I wouldn't hear a lick of it because of all that electricity buzzing around. 

So if you were asking me about something else just now, or if you needed to know something specific for your clipboard there, I really don't know what to tell you. I don't have an answer for you because I just didn't catch a single word of it. I get so wrapped up in the flow of it all, trying so hard to make sure you understand the absolute importance of the baseboards and the way the building is shifting and the signals with the coffee mugs, that I just completely lose track of the actual conversation we're supposed to be having. You're going to have to repeat it for me. What was it you were trying to ask?

Doctor, I apologize, I really do. I know you're trying to do your job, trying to get all the facts straight for my file, and here I am, just running my mouth like a broken faucet that won't shut off. But you see, that's exactly what I mean about the electricity. It just takes over. It's like I'm a passenger in my own body, and the driver has his foot pressed all the way down on the gas pedal, and the brakes are completely shot. 

So, please, I really want to help you figure this out. I want to give you whatever information you need. I just need you to ask me the question again. I promise I'll try my absolute hardest to focus this time, to really listen to what you're saying instead of getting swept away by the current. Just... just tell me what you need to know, and I'll do my best to give you a straight answer, okay? I'm ready now. I'm listening. What was the question?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient exhibits a manic episode (elevated/expansive and irritable mood, grandiosity, decreased need to attend/focus, pressured/tangential speech, increased goal-directed activity, distractibility) that has been present for the majority of the illness course. Critically, he also reports persistent auditory hallucinations ('the man in the vents') and delusions of reference/persecution (coffee mugs, badge taps as 'signals') that continue during 'calm' euthymic periods lasting 2-3 weeks at a time, confirming psychotic symptoms occur in the absence of mood disturbance for a significant period. Because mood episodes (manic) are present for the majority of the total illness duration alongside these psychotic symptoms, and psychotic symptoms persist for ≥2 weeks without prominent mood symptoms, this meets criteria for Schizoaffective Disorder, Bipolar Type (F25.0) rather than Bipolar Disorder with psychotic features (mood-incongruent psychosis outlasting mood episode) or Schizophrenia (mood episodes are prominent and occupy majority of illness duration, not brief/superimposed).
